args.text: --- title: 'Hello World' description: 'Change the FHE computation in the default template so that the E3 returns two times the sum, and run it again.' --- import { Callout, Steps } from 'nextra/components' import { Flow, LinkCard, LinkCards } from '@/components/ui' # Hello World Righto, in this tutorial we're getting our hands dirty: we tweak the FHE computation in the default template and give the E3 another spin. It's for developers who've already been through the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start), so if that's you, you're in the right pub. By the end, your E3 spits out 2 × (a + b) instead of plain old a + b, and you'll know where the computation lives, where its test is, and which bits of the client hold its labels. ## Before you begin You'll want the `my-first-e3` project from the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start), fresh as a daisy, nobody's fiddled with it. Every path on this page is relative to the project folder. ## How the template computes Here's the guts of it: the whole FHE computation is one Rust function, `fhe_processor`, in `program/src/lib.rs`. Everything else in the template is basically the delivery crew, lugging ciphertexts in to this function and carting its result off to the committee. 1. The client encrypts each number with the committee public key and calls `MyProgram.publishInput`. 2. Once the input window slams shut, the coordination server (`server/index.ts`) reads the published inputs and sends them across to the program server on port 13151. 3. The program server (`.interfold/support/dev/src/main.rs`) calls `fhe_processor` and sends the encrypted result back to the coordination server. 4. The coordination server publishes the encrypted result, and the committee decrypts it. Job done. This is the default computation in `program/src/lib.rs`, as it comes out of the box. I've knocked the doc comment above `policy` off here to save a bit of room: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" use e3_compute_provider::{FHEProcessorInput, InputPolicy}; use fhe::bfv::Ciphertext; use fhe_traits::{DeserializeParametrized, Serialize}; pub fn policy() -> InputPolicy { InputPolicy::default() } /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } sum.to_bytes() } ``` - `FHEProcessorInput` has two fields. `ciphertexts` yields `(Vec, u64)` pairs one at a time: the serialized ciphertext and its input index. `params` holds the BFV parameters of the E3. - `Ciphertext::zero` makes the zero ciphertext, the starting value. The `+=` operator adds each input ciphertext onto it. Now here's the clever bit: this addition is homomorphic. The function tots up the hidden values without ever getting a squiz at them. Like counting the takings with the lights off. - `sum.to_bytes()` serializes the encrypted result. - `policy()` returns the input policy. The default policy takes every published input, no questions asked. The template requests E3s with the `insecure-512` parameter set. Its plaintext modulus is 100, so every result gets worked out modulo 100. For this tutorial, 2 × (a + b) has to come in under 100, so go easy on the numbers. ## Change the computation ### Stop the stack If `pnpm dev:all` is still chugging away, hit `Ctrl+C` in its terminal. ### Double the encrypted sum In `program/src/lib.rs`, rip out the `fhe_processor` function and put this version in its place: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" {9-11} /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } // Add the encrypted sum to itself. The hidden value becomes 2 × (a + b). let doubled = &sum + ∑ doubled.to_bytes() } ``` `&sum + &sum` adds two ciphertexts and returns a new ciphertext. And you don't need a single new import. Beauty. ### Update the unit test The test down the bottom of `program/src/lib.rs` encrypts 3 and 2 and calls `fhe_processor`. It's still expecting the old answer, so change the expected value from 5 to 10: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" let tally = Vec::::try_decode(&decrypted, Encoding::poly())?; assert_eq!(tally[0], 10); Ok(()) ``` ### Run the unit test ```bash cargo test -p e3-user-program ``` Cargo prints `test tests::test ... ok`. If the test falls in a heap, put your `fhe_processor` up against the code in the step before and spot the difference. ### Update the label on the input step The maths has changed, so the labels have to catch up. In `client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx`, hunt down this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: {input1} + {input2} = ? ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: 2 × ({input1} + {input2}) = ? ``` ### Update the label on the results step Same drill over in `client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx`. Find this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2} = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `2 × (${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2}) = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` ### Start the stack ```bash pnpm dev:all ``` The `PROGRAM` process runs `interfold program start`. In dev mode, that command runs `cargo run --bin e3-support-scripts-dev`, so Cargo compiles the program server again from scratch with your shiny new `fhe_processor` in it. ### Run an E3 Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). If the client's still showing the result of an earlier E3, select **Start over** in the top bar. Request an E3, then punch in 5 and 3. The input step shows `Ready to compute: 2 × (5 + 3) = ?`. The results step shows `2 × (5 + 3) = 16`. Sixteen, and nobody along the way ever laid eyes on the 5 or the 3. Too easy. ## Why nothing else changes - **The contract.** `MyProgram.publishInput` stores a commitment for each input, and `MyProgram.verify` checks the compute proof. Neither function has the computation in it, so neither one cares. - **The coordination server.** `server/index.ts` sends every published input to the program server and publishes whatever output it gets back. It's just the postie: hasn't got a clue what the computation does. - **The deployment.** `pnpm dev:all` deploys the contracts again on a brand new local chain every time it starts. In dev mode, the program server runs `fhe_processor` without a proof, and the template deploys `MockOpenVmReceiptVerifier`, which waves every receipt on the local chain straight through, like a bouncer who's knocking off in five. With real proofs, though, `MyProgram.verify` checks the OpenVM receipt against the `imageId` that `MyProgram` gets handed when it's deployed. Change the program and that identity changes too, so compile and deploy again. See [Compute provider](/build/e3-program/compute-provider). ## Update the integration test The template's also got an end-to-end test in `tests/integration.spec.ts`. It encrypts 1 and 2 and expects their sum, which isn't the answer any more. So after your change, update the expected value: ```ts filename="tests/integration.spec.ts" expect(BigInt(result)).toBe(2n * (num1 + num2)) ``` Run the test with `pnpm test:integration`. Heads up, but: this test needs a CLI built with the `test-only-skip-proof-aggregation` Cargo feature, and the release binaries don't come with it. See [Installation](/build/installation#install-the-cli) for a source build. ## Operations on ciphertexts So what else can you do to a ciphertext? The template uses the `fhe` crate from `gnosisguild/fhe.rs` at tag `v0.4.2`, and for a `Ciphertext` that crate implements these operators: | Operation | Operator | Example | | --------------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------- | | Add two ciphertexts | `+`, `+=` | `&a + &b` | | Subtract two ciphertexts | `-`, `-=` | `&a - &b` | | Negate a ciphertext | unary `-` | `-&a` | | Add or subtract a plaintext | `+`, `+=`, `-`, `-=` | `&a + &plaintext` | | Multiply by a plaintext | `*`, `*=` | `&a * &plaintext` | A `Plaintext` has to use the same parameters object as the ciphertext, that is, `fhe_inputs.params`. If the parameters objects don't match, the operator panics. Throws a proper wobbly. Every result wraps modulo the plaintext modulus. So a negative result, say from `&a - &b` with `a < b`, wraps right round to a big value. Don't go expecting a minus sign. The crate also implements `*` for two ciphertexts, but the default template doesn't touch it and this page leaves it well alone. ## Next steps Write the FHE computation for your very own E3 program. Validate inputs and verify proofs in your E3 program contract. Track down the file to edit for each bit of the template.
